Encoder Older models like RNNs struggled with long sentences. Example: “The food at the restaurant was terrible… but the dessert was amazing.” The word “amazing” relates to dessert, not food. But they are far apart. Self-attention ﬁxes this by allowing: Every word to directly talk to every other word. Distance becomes irrelevant. This was revolutionary. A Query represents what a word is trying to ﬁnd in the rest of the sentence. You can think of it as a question the word is asking, such as “Which other words are important for my meaning?” When the model processes a token, it generates a Query vector that gets compared with the Key vectors of all other tokens. The stronger the match, the more attention that word receives. In simple terms, the Query is the search signal that helps a word gather the right context before forming a deeper understanding. A Key is like a label that describes what information a word contains and how relevant it might be to others. Every token produces a Key vector, and these keys are checked against incoming Queries to measure compatibility. If a Key closely aligns with a Query, the model interprets that word as important for the current context. Essentially, Keys help answer the question, “Do I have the information you are looking for?” This matching process is what allows the model to identify relationships between words, regardless of how far apart they appear in a sentence. A Value holds the actual information that will be shared once a strong Query–Key match is found. After calculating attention scores, the model does not pass along the Keys or Queries it combines the Value vectors based on how much attention each word deserves. This weighted blending creates a richer, contextual representation of the token. Put simply, if the Query is the question and the Key determines relevance, the Value is the knowledge that gets delivered, enabling the model to understand language in a more connected and meaningful way.
